short: Taiwan's AI Basic Act has been in force since its promulgation on 14 January 2026. It directs the government to build a risk framework and liability rules, and contains no penalties of its own.
title: Taiwan AI Laws
subtitle: The AI Basic Act, a framework law in force since 14 January 2026
body_html:
Status at a glance

AI law in force, without penalties. Taiwan's Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (人工智慧基本法) was passed by the Legislative Yuan on 23 December 2025 and promulgated on 14 January 2026, the day it took effect (Art. 20). It is a framework law: it sets seven principles, makes the National Science and Technology Council the central competent authority, and directs the Ministry of Digital Affairs and the sector regulators to build a risk-based regime, including liability rules for high-risk AI, within two years. It contains no penalties. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the Presidential Office Gazette, the Ministry of Justice laws database and the Legislative Yuan.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberPassedPromulgatedIn force
Artificial Intelligence Basic ActPresidential Order Hua-Zong-Yi-Zi No. 11500001671; Presidential Office Gazette No. 783723 December 202514 January 202614 January 2026 (Art. 20)
Personal Data Protection ActLatest amendment 11 November 2025In force; the amended articles' effective date is to be set by the Executive Yuan (Art. 56)

Who regulates and enforces

  • National Science and Technology Council (NSTC): central competent authority (Art. 2) and staff office for the national AI strategy committee (Art. 6).
  • Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA): builds a risk classification framework aligned with international standards (Art. 16) and, with sector regulators, designates high-risk uses (Art. 5).
  • Sector regulators: write risk-based rules for their sectors (Art. 16).
  • Executive Yuan national AI strategy committee, chaired by the Premier: sets the national AI guidelines (Art. 6).
  • Personal Data Protection Commission: the competent authority under the Personal Data Protection Act (Art. 1-1).

Scope and reach

The Act binds the government, not private parties directly. It defines AI as a system with autonomous operation that produces predictions, content, recommendations or decisions through machine learning and algorithms (Art. 3). It has no extraterritorial provision. Research and development before real-world use is outside the liability regime, except testing in a real environment or providing products or services (Art. 17(2)).

Core obligations

  • Seven principles: sustainability, human autonomy, privacy and data governance, security, transparency and explainability, fairness, and accountability (Art. 4).
  • High-risk AI products or systems, as designated by the sector regulator with MODA, must carry clear notices or warnings (Art. 5(2)).
  • Sector regulators must restrict or prohibit the uses listed in Article 5(1) (Art. 16).
  • The government sets liability, relief, compensation or insurance mechanisms for high-risk AI (Art. 17), avoids unnecessary personal data processing (Art. 14), assesses the risk of its own AI use (Art. 19), and reviews its rules within two years (Art. 18).

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Anything under the AI Basic ActNone: the Act has no penalty provisions
Unlawful use of personal data for gain or to harm, under the Personal Data Protection ActUp to 5 years' imprisonment, with a fine of up to NT$1 millionPDPA Art. 41Courts
Administrative breaches of the PDPA, in its latest textNT$150,000 to NT$15 million per violationPDPA Art. 48 as amended 11 November 2025; whether this ceiling applies yet depends on the amendment's effective date, which is still to be setCompetent authority

What is coming next

  • By 14 January 2028 (two years after entry into force, as this site computes it): the government must amend, enact or repeal the rules that do not conform to the Act (Art. 18).
  • The Executive Yuan to set the effective date of the 2025 Personal Data Protection Act amendments.
